n: The Churchill Rocket Research Range was used beginning in 1954 for sub-orbital launches of sounding rockets to study the upper atmosphere. n: The Atlantic Spaceport Complex (ASX) is a commercial space launch facility in Newfoundland and Labrador, Canada. The launch site is located near the town of St. Lawrence - about 350 kilometers southwest of St. John's. Construction of the facility was announced in August 2025.

n: Andøya Space Center (formerly Andøya Rakettskytefelt) is a is a rocket launch site, rocket range, and spaceport on Andøya island (the northernmost in the Vesterålen archipelago) in the Andøy Municipality. Since 1962, over 1,200 sounding and sub-orbital rockets of various configurations have been launched from the site.

n: Edwards Air Force Base is a United States Air Force installation in California. Edwards is the home of the Air Force Test Center, Air Force Test Pilot School, and NASA's Armstrong Flight Research Center. It is the Air Force Materiel Command center for conducting and supporting research and development of flight, as well as testing and evaluating aerospace systems from concept to combat. It also hosts many test activities conducted by America's commercial aerospace industry. Notable occurrences at Edwards include Chuck Yeager's flight that broke the sound barrier in the Bell X-1, test flights of the North American X-15, the first landings of the Space Shuttle, and the 1986 around-the-world flight of the Rutan Voyager.

n: Originally an admittedly boring magnet company, Clamp-O-Tron expanded into the aerospace industry after an engineer suggested using their magnets to "stick things together... but in SPACE!". The famed Clamp-O-Tron Docking Port has received numerous collaborations with well-known conglomerates, such as C7 Aerospace Division, to help bring the joy of clamping things together to your own space program and beyond. Clamp-O-Tron representatives would also like to remind the general public to "Please stop leaving our products on the side of the road", and to browse their online catalog instead if they wish to purchase any of their world-renowned docking ports.

n: For when you find yourself free-falling through life (or out of a malfunctioning rocket), FreeFall Parachutes has you covered. Metaphorically, that is. From skydiving on Kerbin to landing probes on distant worlds, their parachutes are the go-to option for any budding space program. Despite their insistence on using 100% reclaimed materials for their chutes, having the brand is generally recognized as being a better option than lithobraking. They boast a generous policy on all their products: Any chute that fails to open during flight can be returned after landing for a partial refund! This policy has proven to be surprisingly unpopular with KSC astronauts, for some reason. FreeFall executives are still working on why that is.

n: The major competitor with Kerbal Motion LLC in the "Round Wheels" market, LightYear Tire Company provides Piston Cup-rated rubber tires to the space center, at wholesale prices nonetheless. If you've ever smelled the sweet, sweet scent of burning rubber on the KSC tarmac, there's a good chance that it was from a LightYear tire. Their range of products includes multiple sizes of space-grade landing gear - shock absorbers and spotlights included at no additional cost, their brochure advertises. LightYear is currently locked in a struggle with C7 Aerospace as the conglomerate repeatedly attempts to acquire the company. LightYear is one of the few independent manufacturers left that hasn't been absorbed by the titan of the aerospace world.

n: Originally part of Jebediah Kerman's Junkyard and Spacecraft Parts Co., the Stratus Corporation has only recently left the nest to pursue bigger goals out in the aerospace world. While not the largest fuel supplier in the market, Stratus earned its reputation by cementing itself as one of the few manufacturers to experiment with Monopropellant. They've effectively cornered the market due to the apparent lack of interest in this fuel type. Regardless, they currently have a lucrative deal with the KSC to supply all Monopropellant fuel for our astronauts' EVA packs and command pods. Their flagship line, the 'Stratus-V' series of tanks, won them several awards at last year's 3rd annual Fuel Tanks & Swimming Pools Expo.

n: A large-size fallback-type service tower inspired by the transporter-erector used for the Falcon 9. It has two methods of fallback retraction: A simple one-step type which fully retracts the tower, activated by staging only, and a two-step manual method in which the tower can be first partially retracted by a small amount before launch, followed by a seprate fallback retract for liftoff. The tower has 3 height and 2 color options. The upper clamp has two size options, or can be turned off, and can be adjusted vertically with its deploy limit slider. The fixed umbilicals are moved vertically with the upper clamp, and their length can be adjusted with their deploy limit slider, or turned off. From Modular Launch Pad mod

The arm can be adjusted in length by using the deploy limit slider. Animation can be either staged or done manually/action-grouped. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: Large-size animated general swing arm for the general and specialty towers, available in 8 colors. The arm swing can be done in the default or alternate direction by using the appropriate toggle; arm swing done by staging is only in the default direction. The umbilical connectors can be switched between conventional end type and Delta IV side type; side type can be on either side of the arm depending on arm swing direction. The end connecters have 5 style options, and the side connectors can be tall or short, with the center and outer sets separately toggleable. Each of the arm pipes can be switched among 4 colors. The arm can be adjusted in length by using the deploy limit slider. The spacing of the outer umbilical rails for the side style can be decreased using its deploy limit slider. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: Animated twin vertical retracting umbilical arms for the Centaur upper stage used on the Atlas SLV-3 Centaur D rocket. The arms bracket the Centaur stage, with the bottom arm straddling the interdstage-tank division, and the upper arm stradding the tank-fairing junction. Designed to mount on the Atlas-Centaur Service Tower, but can be used with other towers as well. The whole arm frame assembly can be adjusted upward by using the offset gizmo for fine positioning. The upper tall arm (Arm 1) can be adjusted in both horizontal and vertical position using the deploy limit sliders. The lower flat arm can be adjusted horizontally with its slider. The arms and frame also have 8 color options. The arms can be retracted either by manual toggling the animation or by staging. Use with the Atlas Launch Stand for best effect. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: A crew access elevator for small manned spacecraft, inspired by the emergency egress and umbilical tower used for Mercury-Atlas and designed for the Tier 1 launch pad and the Atlas Launch Stand, but can be used with some other launch bases and stands. The elevator tower is a fixed type, with 8 colors available. The stopping height of the elevator car is adjusted with a deploy limit slider. Use with the Mercury-Atlas Elevator Crew Walkway, which attaches to one of the front nodes, and flips up to retract. The separate Mercury Umbilical Mast attaches to a node on the front platform of the tower. Hatch on the elevator car allows an alternate method of travel. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: A crew access elevator for Gemini spacecraft, inspired by the erector used for the Titan II-Gemini. Designed for use with the mtaching Titan II Launch Stand, but also can be used with other Launch Stands, Plates and Bases. The elevator tower fits around the Titan II or other rocket, with the access floor in the top white room fitting close to the capsule. Both the elevator car maximum height and the access floor height can be adjusted with their deploy limit sliders so they match up with each other. The elevator tower has three height variants, and is a downward rotating type, with an exterior elevator car. The front white panels on the tower can be retracted if desired. There is only one color option for the tower. Hatches on the elevator car allow an alternate method of travel. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: Add-on part for launch bases and stands that provides a rotatable launch rail for angled launching of rockets. This is the Large size rail, meant for larger rockets of size 1.25m and up. Rockets are only surface-attached to the rail, and the rail has built-in a decoupler. The rail can also be switched between the default forward direction and reverse. Rotating the rail can be done with the B9PD switcher or optionally with Animated Attachment installed via the deploy limit slider animation. The Animated Attachment method requires that the rail or launch base/stand be the root part in order to move the attached rocket. The rail part however can not be the root part after rotation or it will not decouple from the rocket. The rail can be rotated 100 degrees in the forward direction or 20 degrees in the reverse direction. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: This is the free-standing base for the Saturn Mobile Launcher. The base attaches to a free node in the center of a rocket's lower or core stage using the size 5 node at the top of the exhaust hole opening. The tower base section attaches to the size 5 node on the other end of the launcher base. Includes a built-in decoupler and an elevator for crew access from the ground to the top deck. For best results, put the front legs so that they are inside the white part of the big circle on the VAB floor. No launch clamps are necessary. Includes a manually-activated generator for electric charge. The base's exhaust hole can be configured for three sizes of rockets: Saturn V (6.4/5.625m), SLS (5m) and the Saturn IB (4.25/3.75m), with various square and rectangular shapes for either single-core or tri-core rockets. A variety of switchable hold-down arm support configurations are available, along with optional center-mount hold-down and Saturn V tail service mast attach nodes. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: The "Milkstool", as it was nicknamed, was a stand created to allow the Saturn IB-Apollo to use the Saturn V's Launch Umbilical Tower on LC 39. The three Skylab crews and the Apollo CSM for the Apollo-Soyuz Test Project were launched from LC 39 with the milkstool. In reality it was a gray color, but a red variant is also available as an alternative. Attach the milkstool to a bottom center node of a rocket, then attach the launcher base to the bottom node of the milkstool. The center ring at top has switchable hold-down arm support and node arrangements. There is a built-in decoupler for separating the milkstool from a rocket for liftoff. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: Small size launch base for the Space Shuttle, made for smaller flat launch pads, and inspired by the launch mount for the shuttle at Vandenberg's SLC-6 pad. The base attaches to the shuttle's External Tank via the large node in the center, and requires a free attach node below the center of the shuttle's External Tank in order to be attached. Service towers are attached to the nodes around the outside of the mount. SRB hold-downs are integrated into the base and are adjusted with the deploy limit sliders. The shuttle tail service masts attach on the sides of the square main engine exhaust hole, either with the two nodes or by surface attach. The whole base can be rotated via the switcher to keep the support legs in the right place. From Modular Launch Pad mod

n: A very expensive and fragile, but also very light tank. Balloon tanks are expensive and complex as they need to be pressurized at all times, but they are much lighter than regular tanks. These are similar to tanks used on the Atlas and Centaur stages. The first balloon tanks are 73% lighter than Al stringer conventional structure tanks while costing 150% more to tool and 60% more once tooled. Min Utilization: 99% - Max Utilization: 100% From RealFuels mod

n: A more complex, but lightweight tank. Isogrid structure tanks use machined walls that are also load-bearing and form the entire structure of the tank, so no additional structure is needed to maintain rigidity. Manufacturing them can be difficult, however. The first level of isogrid tanks are 40% (standard) or 55% (HP) lighter than Al stringer conventional structure tanks while costing 50% more to tool and 40% more once tooled. From RealFuels mod

n: The most basic form of fuel tank. Conventional structure tanks consist of two parts, a support structure (also known as stringers) and a fuel tank. This makes them cheap and easy to produce. From RealFuels mod

n: RD-0410 was a Soviet nuclear thermal rocket engine developed from 1965 through the 1994 using liquid hydrogen propellant. The engine was ground-tested at the Semipalatinsk Test Site, and its use was incorporated in the Kurchatov Mars 1994 manned mission proposal. Its moderator and fuel are quite different from the US designs and Metal Carbide (MC) versions of the fuel are rumoured to have reach as high as 3500K without melting in the early 1990's. Use of Heptane to reduce hydrogen corrosion of the carbides was critical to function (~1%). First run tests occurred in 1985. Some Russian sources list it as dual mode using not only Hydrogen but also liquid Methane without additives. During the SNTP program the US tried to acquire MC fuels from Russian sources but planned purchases fell through. This engine is very heavily built compared to US designs and incorporates a four lobed spiral fuel rod to eliminate risk of fuel being ejected if the rods shattered. This design uses a short regeneratively cooled nozzle and is intended as an upper stage. Design stats Nozzle Ae=46 Chamber Temp=3000 Ideal ISP=972 Reactor Power=173MW(th) TWR=1.73 Chamber Pressure=4000kPa Ignitions =10 Tonnage including integral shadow shield:2tons. In Methane mode the nozzle is slightly expanded by 12cm length and slightly enlarged. Nozzle Ae=46 Chamber Temp=3000 Ideal ISP=467 Reactor Power=173MW(th) TWR=3.56 Chamber Pressure=4800kPa Ignitions =10 Tonnage including integral shadow shield:2tons From ReStock Plus mod

n: The abort motor of the LES is a powerful solid rocket motor, designed specifically to carry away the Apollo Command Module in the case of a pad or a low altitude flight abort. n: Dynasoar cockpit. Dynasoar (short for "Dynamic Soarer") was an early USAF spaceplane, intended to function as a station tender, reconnaissance craft, and nuclear bomber. Designed for "Dynamic Soaring", dipping deep into the atmosphere and using aerodynamic manuevers to skip back out, or change it's orbit. n: Low thrust pump-fed expander nuclear engine. n: The Castor 4 was developed as the second stage of the Athena H missile and first flew in 1971. It was later adapted to replace Delta's Castor 2 boosters, increasing GTO capacity from 723 kg to nearly 900 kg. The Delta 3000-series launched in 1975 with a staggered booster staging sequence. Previous Deltas burned their motors in a 6-3 sequence and then jettisoned all SRMs at once. The heavier and longer-burning Castor 4 required that the motors be jettisoned as soon as they ran out to reduce dead weight. A less efficient 5-4 sequence was used until Delta was strengthened in the early 80s to handle the acceleration of a 6-3 sequence. From ROEngines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall and SmokeScreen.

n: The Castor 4A was introduced on the first generation of Delta II launchers, the 6000-series, and offered improved thrust and specific impulse by replacing PBAA with higher energy HTPB. This, combined with a stretched first stage (the Extra-Extended Long Tank Thor), and a return to the more efficient 6-3 SRM ignition sequence, improved Delta's performance by 11% over the 3000-series. The Castor 4A was flown on the Delta II from 1989 until 1993, when it was replaced by the GEM 40. The boosters were also used on the Atlas IIAS from 1993 until 2004. Burn time 53 seconds. From ROEngines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall and SmokeScreen.

n: The "Nerva XE" series is a 1550 MW reactor. A full flight test prototype originally based on the KIWI B4E. Its core is capable of starting up sixty times. An integral Tungsten Boron composite shield is included and the whole assembly is regeneratively cooled. A secondary circuit runs the shut down gasses through a small heat engine to minimize fuel loss and provide basic alternator power. This engine should be mounted three to six meters from the closest fuel tank. Fuel should shield any crew and crew positions when running should be eight to ten meters from the engine. Additional shielding such as a water tank or high density fuel can somewhat reduce this amount. This rocket represents the beginnings of a more powerful and capable series of rocket. This version features a fixed regeneratively cooled nozzle with a 100:1 expansion ratio. n: The first multi-chamber engine developed by Glushko. After Glushko's attempts to scale up existing engines for what would become the R-7 resulted in unresolvable combustion instability (RD-105/106), Glushko instead combined multiple chambers of his ED-140 engine into one to increase thrust. The result, the RD-200, proved successful and, although it never flew, its design formed the basis of the RD-107/108 and RD-214. From ROEngines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall.

n: A Soviet hypergolic staged combustion engine. Developed as part of an initiative to build a 150-ton-thrust vacuum engine for the N1, versions were created burning nitric acid, NTO, or LOX with UDMH. Although the NK-15V was ultimately selected to power the N1, the RD-254, using NTO, was chosen to power the upper stages of the UR-700. The RD-254 was cancelled with the rest of the UR-700 project and never flew. From ROEngines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall.

n: The world's first closed-cycle engine. The S1.5400 was used as the final stage for the R-7's Molniya configuration to launch communication satellites and interplanetary probes. Unlike prior upper stages, it was restartable (apogee kicks are needed for Molniya orbits). It was given the industry designation 11D33. The 11D33M brought upgrades and was the basis for the RD-58 with higher performance still (designated 11D58). The RD-58 was used on many Russian launchers, including N1 and Buran and is still in use on Proton and Zenit. From ROEngines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall.

n: The H-1 is an upgrade to the original LR79 engine that propelled the Saturn-I and IB vehicles, as well as late-model Delta rockets (as the RS-27). n: A 1990s atmospheric engine using technology developed for the Space Shuttle SSME, the RS-68 is a single-use engine. n: The "SNTP-PFE" series is a 1000MW reactor. The reactor is a particle bed using metallic carbide coated uranium granules embedded in a graphite rod that hydrogen is passed through. This allows for power densities of up to 40MW/liter. Its core is capable of starting up five times. An integral Tungsten Boron Lithium Hydride composite shield is included and the whole assembly is regeneratively cooled. A secondary circuit runs the shut down gasses through a small heat engine to minimize fuel loss and provide basic alternator power. This engine should be mounted three to six meters from the closest fuel tank. Fuel should shield any crew and crew positions when running should be ten to fifteen meters from the engine. Additional shielding such as a water tank or high density fuel can somewhat reduce this amount. This rocket has impressive stats for its size (Nozzle Ae=100 Chamber Temp=3000 Ideal ISP=991 Reactor Power=1054MW(th) TWR=13.94 Chamber Pressure=6800kPa Ignitions =5 Tonnage including integral shadow shield:1.504tons ) The nozzle is a fixed ablatively cooled filament wound carbon-carbon design. From ROEngines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall.

n: The most basic form of fuel tank. Conventional structure tanks consist of two parts, a support structure (also known as stringers) and a fuel tank. Earlier iterations also had a separate skin surrounding them, but later tanks moved the structure inside the fuel tanks, making the tanks integral to the vehicle structure. This makes them cheap and easy to produce. From ROTanks mod

n: A more complex, but lightweight tank. Isogrid structure tanks use machined walls that are also load-bearing and form the entire structure of the tank, so no additional structure is needed to maintain rigidity. Manufacturing them can be difficult, however. The first level of isogrid tanks are 40% (standard) or 55% (HP) lighter than Al stringer conventional structure tanks while costing 50% more to tool and 40% more once tooled. From ROTanks mod

n: A late 50s turbojet based on the Pratt & Whitney J57, the Model 304-2 was a liquid-hydrogen-fueled turbojet, designed for project SUNTAN, a high-performance replacement for the U-2 spyplane. The project required the development of large-scale liquid hydrogen production and handling techniques, at the cost of hundreds of millions of dollars. Various jet engines were converted to hydrogen power, where they showed incredible stability and efficiency. This information, along with many of the engineers involved, were later transferred to working on the RL-10 where the information gained proved invaluable. The Model 304 and project SUNTAN, however, were ultimately cancelled, as the conventionally-fueled A-12/SR-71 was showing much greater promise. From Advanced Jet Engines mod

n: The AL-31 is a early 1980s low-bypass turbofan, designed to power the Su-27. n: An early 1960s nuclear turbo-ramjet, designed for supersonic bombers. One of the ultimate direct-cycle designs produced by the Aircraft Nuclear Propulsion (ANP) program, the A-136 used a hybrid cycle to improve supersonic performance. By tapping off a small amount of air to cool the turbine, turbine inlet temperatures could be managed, while the remaining air passed straight through the reactor and was heated to full temperature. This gave the engine good performance up to Mach 3. It also included a kerosene burner to improve takeoff thrust. From Advanced Jet Engines mod Plume and sound from Waterfall.

n: RD-0410 was a Soviet nuclear thermal rocket engine developed from 1965 through the 1994 using liquid hydrogen propellant. The engine was ground-tested at the Semipalatinsk Test Site, and its use was incorporated in the Kurchatov Mars 1994 manned mission proposal. Its moderator and fuel are quite different from the US designs and Metal Carbide (MC) versions of the fuel are rumoured to have reach as high as 3500K without melting in the early 1990's. Use of Heptane to reduce hydrogen corrosion of the carbides was critical to function (~1%). First run tests occurred in 1985. Some Russian sources list it as dual mode using not only Hydrogen but also liquid Methane without additives. During the SNTP program the US tried to acquire MC fuels from Russian sources but planned purchases fell through. This engine is very heavily built compared to US designs and incorporates a four lobed spiral fuel rod to eliminate risk of fuel being ejected if the rods shattered. This design uses a short regeneratively cooled nozzle and is intended as an upper stage. Design stats Nozzle Ae=46 Chamber Temp=3000 Ideal ISP=972 Reactor Power=173MW(th) TWR=1.73 Chamber Pressure=4000kPa Ignitions =10 Tonnage including integral shadow shield:2tons. In Methane mode the nozzle is slightly expanded by 12cm length and slightly enlarged. Nozzle Ae=46 Chamber Temp=3000 Ideal ISP=467 Reactor Power=173MW(th) TWR=3.56 Chamber Pressure=4800kPa Ignitions =10 Tonnage including integral shadow shield:2tons From Bornholio Nuclear mod Plume and sound from Waterfall.

n: The "Phoebus 2" series is a 5000MW reactor. Most tests resulted in success proving new coatings worked well and existing at the time as the most powerful reactor core on the planet. Its core is capable of starting up eight times. An integral Tungsten Boron composite shield is included and the whole assembly is regeneratively cooled. A secondary circuit runs the shut down gasses through a small heat engine to minimize fuel loss and provide basic alternator power. This engine should be mounted three to six meters from the closest fuel tank. Fuel should shield any crew and crew positions when running should be ten to fifteen meters from the engine. Additional shielding such as a water tank or high density fuel can somewhat reduce this amount. This rocket represents a more powerful and capable series of rocket with a TWR of nearly 6. This version features a fixed regeneratively cooled nozzle with a 100:1 expansion ratio.
